entries.title: Where voters stand on state ballot measures, from abortion to LGBTQ rights to guns
entries.summary: Voters in dozens of states considered 146 statewide ballot measures this midterm cycle, on topics spanning LGBTQ rights, wealth taxes, abortion, redistricting, guns and more.
entries.content:
Where voters stand on state ballot measures, from abortion to LGBTQ rights to guns

Tuesday's midterm elections were a huge sweep for Democrats, among other takeaways.

And across 39 states — plus Washington, D.C. and the Northern Mariana Islands — voters weighed in on 146 statewide ballot measures spanning issues from taxes to transgender rights to traffic cameras to data centers and AI.

Here's a look at some of those results.

Three states moved to preserve abortion access

The U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, leaving the legality and regulation of abortion up to each state. In subsequent elections, over a dozen states have put access to abortion on their ballots — and overwhelmingly moved to secure it.

This year, four states considered abortion measures. Three passed, while Idaho voted to preserve the state's abortion ban from 2022.

In Missouri, voters rejected a Republican-led amendment that would have banned abortion with few exceptions. The move affirms support for abortion just two years after voters mobilized to reject Missouri's ban, which was one of the strictest in the country.

Loading...

Nevada residents voted to enshrine abortion up to the point of viability in their constitution. They did so for the second election in a row, since state law requires a proposed constitutional amendment to pass twice.

Virginians voted to create a "fundamental right to reproductive freedom" in their constitution. That includes the right to an abortion during the first two trimesters (and afterward in certain cases), as well as the right to contraception, fertility, postpartum care and more.

States voted on voting

Many states considered changes to how they run their elections.

It was too early to call Wednesday afternoon whether voters had approved some of the more far-reaching changes, in Alaska and Arizona.

Other states — including Nevada, North Carolina and Ohio — passed measures toughening identification requirements for voters, while California voted against such an effort.

Several states — including Alaska, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia — approved measures reinforcing that U.S. citizenship is required to vote in their elections.

Redistricting was also top of mind for voters. President Trump kicked off a redistricting race earlier this year by urging Republican-led states to redraw their districts ahead of the midterms. Republicans and Democrats in multiple states did so. But many of the districts altered to boost GOP prospects ultimately went to Democratic candidates.

Missouri voters rejected a Republican-friendly congressional map, while Maryland voters passed a redistricting amendment that could pave the way for a Democrat-leaning map in 2028.

Loading...

Virginians passed a measure automatically restoring voting rights to anyone convicted of a felony once they have completed their sentence.

A mixed bag for LGBTQ rights

Virginians also passed a constitutional amendment officially repealing its ban on gay marriage and adding language confirming that the commonwealth will recognize marriage between two adults regardless of their sex, gender or race.

Virginia's ban has been moot since the Supreme Court made same-sex marriage legal nationwide in 2015, but this measure is seen as a safeguard in case Obergefell v. Hodges gets reversed (as some have feared in the wake of the court's overturning of Roe v. Wade). Other states have made similar moves, including Colorado and California in 2024.

Vermont overwhelmingly voted to add an amendment to its constitution guaranteeing equal protection under the law "race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, or national origin."

A number of states considered measures restricting transgender kids' access to school sports teams and gender-affirming care, with Colorado passing both. A Washington state measure to ban trans students from competing in girls' school sports was still leading on Wednesday.

Arizona passed a proposal requiring schools and athletic associations to restrict students, athletes and employees from using facilities — including restrooms, locker rooms, and other private spaces — that are not designated for their sex assigned at birth. Arizona law already bans trans girls from playing on school sports teams designated for girls, and this measure would extend that prohibition to recreational organizations like Little League.

Loading...

Taxes and state spending up for debate

One of the most high-profile ballot measures asked Floridians to weigh cutting property taxes for homeowners, which critics say would take billions of dollars in local government revenue away from much-needed public services like food banks, libraries, transportation and infrastructure. Voters overwhelmingly passed the amendment.

In California, voters pondered whether to approve a one-off 5% tax on individuals with more than $1 billion in assets, with most of the money raised going toward health care services. The fight against that ballot measure was one of the most expensive in the state's history. The contest is too close to call as of Wednesday afternoon.

Loading...

Tennessee voters approved a constitutional amendment prohibiting its government from levying a statewide property tax, which it has not collected since 1949. Arizona voters passed a measure that bans cities and towns from raising taxes on groceries until July 2027. North Carolinians approved an amendment to cap the maximum personal income tax at 3.5%.

Washington voters considered whether to repeal an income tax on individuals and households earning more than $1 million, which is scheduled to take effect in 2028. Early results indicate they want to keep that tax.

A polar-opposite pair of gun ballot measures

Massachusetts voted to keep a 2024 law tightening firearm regulations. The law made Massachusetts gun control measures among the strictest in the nation, as it also included requiring "ghost guns" to have a serial number, broadened the definition of "assault-style firearm" and expanded the state's red flag laws.

Meanwhile, in Idaho, a ballot measure asked voters for help choosing the official state gun from six different brands and models. The Winchester Model 1873 — aka the "Gun that Won the West" — leads in the polls as of Wednesday, though the state legislature would need to pass a separate law to make the winner official.

The ballot initiatives about data centers

At least 38 jurisdictions voted on the sprawling facilities needed to power AI, and Tuesday revealed how many voters dislike them. Jurisdictions in California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota, Ohio, and Wisconsin voted to restrict data centers.

Of these, at least 12 localities voted to restrict the size of data centers, while six others voted to halt development and ban construction of all facilities, according to Data Centers on the Ballot.

The one community that supported data centers is in Harwood, North Dakota, where 75% of voters did not want to place restrictions on industrial projects, including data centers.

Ohio, one of the frontline states on the issue, had 21 ballot measures mentioning data centers. Voters there moved to restrict the AI facilities: Trenton, Ohio voted to ban data centers over 25 megawatts, while Hubbard moved to ban construction of data centers of any size, including converting existing buildings. Ohio voters also rejected rezoning areas from rural residential to light industrial for data center usage.

Candidates spent up to $40 million on ads about data centers this election cycle. They were a contentious issue in many statewide elections, as 77% of Americans say they are concerned about data centers raising electricity costs, according to a June Reuters/Ipsos poll. The poll also showed two-thirds of Democrats and half of Republicans said they'd oppose a data center in their community.

Other honorable mentions

Alabama voters passed ballot measures requiring local school boards to adopt policies directing public K-12 schools to recite the Pledge of Allegiance and, separately, play or perform the first stanza of "The Star-Spangled Banner" at least once a week during school hours.

In Arizona, voters passed a measure banning the state from installing and using photo enforcement systems (like speed and red-light cameras) to catch people who violate certain traffic ordinances.

Residents of Washington, D.C. had just one ballot initiative to consider: banning the controversial duck or goose liver dish known as foie gras. The debate went viral in recent days, prompting a slew of Halloween costumes, a four-course restaurant tasting menu and public appearances by a real duck named Olivia. D.C. voted overwhelmingly to prohibit the force-feeding of birds to enlarge their livers, and the sale of the delicacy itself. Across the country, voters in Denver approved a similar measure.

entries.title: Elon Musk will face scrutiny from Democrats after midterms
entries.summary: Democrats are likely to launch investigations into Musk's influence, including his leadership of DOGE and government contracts
entries.content:
Elon Musk will face scrutiny from Democrats after midterms

Elon Musk wasn't on Tuesday's ballot, but he stands to lose a lot from Democrats' sweeping midterm victories in the House and Senate. In no state was this more acutely felt than in Texas, home to the headquarters of Musk's companies and where he spent more than $200 million, according to federal filings, in a mission to sway the Senate race in the Republican candidate's favor.

With a Democratic majority in Congress, the billionaire, who controls Tesla and SpaceX, will likely face investigations into the billions of dollars of government contracts his companies have been awarded since President Trump returned to office and his role leading the Department of Government Efficiency at the beginning of Trump's second term.

Musk gave more than $445 million to Republican candidates, political action committees and outside groups, according to federal election filings analyzed by OpenSecrets, a nonprofit that tracks campaign spending. That makes him the top donor in the midterms and among the very largest political donors in American history.

The central question Democratic lawmakers say they want answered is whether Musk used his influence inside the Trump administration to benefit his own businesses, and whether taxpayer money, government data and public institutions were put at risk in the process.

During the four months Musk led DOGE, he received at least $6.3 billion in government contracts. Since then, he has gained at least another $10 billion in government contracts, according to the Democracy Defenders Fund, a legal advocacy nonprofit.

"The DOGE chickens are coming home to roost. Elon Musk waved a chainsaw on stage and laughed while firing public servants and gutting the services Americans rely on. Then he lied to the American people about the savings. He must answer for it under oath," Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.) wrote on X.

Musk's foreign dealings are also under scrutiny. Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware posted on X that Musk's links to Russia's President Vladimir Putin are "One more thing to add to the list of questions for Musk when I subpoena him."

U.S. Rep. Mike Levin of California highlighted that Musk restricted Ukraine's use of his Starlink satellite internet service days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia and began buying Russian diesel in October. Starlink and its military-grade counterpart, Starshield, are vital for Ukraine's civilian infrastructure, frontline communications and drone operations in its war against Russia.

"How on earth did we get to this point? How is it possible that Musk can disrupt an American ally's military operations whenever he chooses, maintain a clear line to the Kremlin, and face zero accountability to the American people or the U.S. government?" Levin wrote on X.

Musk did not respond to a request for comment from NPR.

While leading DOGE, Musk was a part-time special government employee, and as such was subject to a federal law prohibiting covered executive branch and related personnel from participating in official matters affecting their personal financial interests, said Richard Painter, former chief White House ethics lawyer in the George W. Bush administration.

"SpaceX is a big contractor and gets a lot of money from NASA and the Department of Defense. If [Musk] touched anything that he knew would have an impact on SpaceX, he would've committed a crime," Painter said.

Texas has played a growing role in Musk's business empire

Texas in particular has become a big focus of Musk's efforts to exert political power, as he has made the state the nerve center of his sprawling business empire. Tesla's corporate headquarters and a major vehicle manufacturing facility are in Austin. X, formerly Twitter, is based outside of Austin. SpaceX, which makes rockets and satellites, is based in southern Texas. Musk's Neuralink and The Boring Company are also headquartered in the state.

Much of Musk's estimated wealth is tied up in his ownership stakes in his companies. Even as markets rose Wednesday after Democrats' midterm wins, SpaceX shares fell nearly 4% and Tesla dropped 3%.

SpaceX is reportedly exploring several possible Texas sites for large data centers. Tesla owns and operates its massive Giga Texas data center in Austin. In August, plans for a $16.8 billion SpaceXAI semiconductor fabrication project in Texas were announced.

Musk directed at least $225 million of his midterm spending to Texas, according to OpenSecrets, including supporting Republican Ken Paxton's bid for U.S. Senate and Gov. Greg Abbott's reelection campaign.

But Paxton and Abbott both lost, suggesting Musk's money wasn't enough to overcome a wave of enthusiasm that saw Democrats capture every statewide office in Texas.

"Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator. He is trying to buy Texas," said James Talarico, who defeated Paxton in the Senate race, at a campaign rally in Lubbock last month.

Elon Musk's own posts on X about Talarico were often personal and incendiary. "Talarico will vote to trans your kids," he wrote on Nov. 1.

Talarico addressed Musk in his victory speech on Tuesday.

"We just sent a message to every billionaire mega-donor, every trillionaire mega-donor, every corrupt defender of this broken political system in this state, in this country. Power belongs to the people," Talarico said. "The real fight in this country is not right versus left; it is top versus bottom."

As results came in on Tuesday night, Musk wrote on X, "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," followed by a shrug emoji.

entries.title: Democratic leaders reflect on midterm results and what's next for the party
entries.summary: Democratic party leaders and political analysts spoke with Morning Edition about the results of the midterm elections, the effects of mid-decade redistricting efforts, and the next steps for the party.
entries.content:
Democratic leaders reflect on midterm results and what's next for the party

Democrats coasted into victory late last night, taking control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate by considerable margins. Several states that are traditionally characterized as "deep red," including Texas, Kansas and Iowa, flipped towards Democrats in the Senate for the first time in decades. Democratic candidates also took a convincing majority in House races, despite competing in several states whose districts were redrawn to favor Republicans.

Across the country, Democratic gubernatorial candidates also burst ahead, winning races in GOP strongholds like Georgia, Ohio and Texas. Heading into 2027, Democrats will officially retake control of Congress and hold at least 28 governorships.

Newly elected Democratic officials, party leaders and pollsters joined Morning Edition on Wednesday morning to share their insights on the massive wave of Democratic victories in state and local races. In their interviews with NPR's Steve Inskeep and Michel Martin, these Democrats discussed takeaways from the midterm results, the effects of mid-decade redistricting efforts, the mandate received from voters and the next steps for the party. You can read some key takeaways from the discussions below.

Abdul El-Sayed

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed made history in Michigan, becoming the first Muslim elected to the Senate as Democrats retake control of Congress. He said his opponent, Republican Mike Rogers, campaigned weaponizing El-Sayed's name and faith rather than addressing issues Americans really care about, like Medicare for All and the price of everyday items.

El-Sayed also discussed his opinions on legislation surrounding the war in Iran, and he agreed with Trump's scheduled end to roughly $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel.

Martin asked him about his lack of support from some Jewish and Black voters, something El Sayed said he hopes to remedy.

"There's always more work to do. There's always more to build. There's always more conversations to have," he said.

To listen to Abdul El-Sayed's full Morning Edition interview, click here.

Eric Holder

Eric Holder, chairman of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee and attorney general under former President Obama, discussed how mid-decade redistricting affected the results of the midterm. Speaking with Martin, he said that GOP gerrymandering efforts backfired, causing candidates to lose in districts that were specifically drawn for their success.

"The redistricting efforts that [Republicans] had didn't just fail — they were dismantled," Holder says.

To listen to Eric Holder's full Morning Edition interview, click here.

Stacey Abrams

Democrats in Georgia won seats up and down the ballot, and Stacey Abrams, founder of Fair Fight Action, said the party has been building towards this outcome since 2010. In her interview with Martin, she added that she's proud of Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black woman elected governor in United States history. Abrams campaigned for the same gubernatorial spot in 2018 and again in 2020, though she was never elected to the position.

Abrams said Democratic victories for the governor, attorney general, secretary of state and in the state house "gives us an opportunity to start correcting and restoring rights that we've seen lost across the South for more than 20 years."

To listen to Stacey Abram's full Morning Edition interview, click here.

Ken Martin

Ken Martin, chairman of the Democratic National Committee, said yesterday's election marks the biggest win for his party in more than a century. Voters gave Democrats a mandate to address affordability, health care and the systems that exclusively benefit wealthy Americans, he explained to Martin and Inskeep, and he thinks newly elected Democrats can deliver.

"Our candidates across the board ran for something, not against something," he said. "They gave people a sense of a positive vision of what Democrats would do while we're in power."

To listen to Ken Martin's full Morning Edition interview, click here.

Margie Omero

Pollster and Democratic strategist Margie Omero explained why last night's results are a direct reflection of voter's distrust of leaders in Washington. She said contested races consistently broke towards Democrats, despite high GOP spending during campaign season.

"Voters really wanted to send a real clear message, and they couldn't have been any clearer than what we heard last night," Omero said.

To listen to Margie Omero's full Morning Edition interview, click here.

entries.title: It was a big night for doctors to win seats in Congress, riding the blue wave
entries.summary: Historically, most physicians who served in the House or Senate have been Republicans. In the next Congress, physicians who are Democrats made significant gains.
entries.content:
It was a big night for doctors to win seats in Congress, riding the blue wave

The U.S. Senate will soon have a practicing physician who's a Democrat for the first time since 1938, with the election of Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in South Carolina.

Her win — among many other physician candidates Tuesday night — marks a dramatic shift when it comes to doctors with political power across the country. Historically, doctors have been elected to Congress more often as Republicans, not Democrats. But that changed this cycle.

Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.

In the recent past, the Republican party attracted doctor-candidates who were essentially small business people who had concerns about high taxes and government overreach. The new crop of candidates from health professions often work for large hospital systems and are interested in issues that align with Democratic priorities like public health, equity and affordability.

Andrews told NPR before she won that she was motivated to enter politics after watching parents worry about the cost of things like inhalers for asthma patients and insulin for kids with diabetes.

"I watch as worried parents leave the hospital in the evening so that they can go work their third shift job just so they can make ends meet," she said. "And then, like the majority of pediatricians in America, I've cared for kids who've been shot." Guns are the leading cause of death for children in the U.S.

"It really clicked to me that the path to catalyzing this change that I want to see in America for the children in America is through politics," she explained.

Blue wins, red losses

In the current Senate, all four of the physicians are Republicans. Two of them, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R.-La., and Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan, lost their reelection bids this year. With the election of South Carolina's Andrews and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, in Michigan, there will now be an equal number of Republican and Democratic physicians in the upper chamber. (El-Sayed trained as a physician but did not do a residency or practice medicine, instead pursuing public health.)

In the House, the six members of the Democratic doctor's caucus will be joined by at least two more: New Jersey's Dr. Adam Hamawy, a former U.S. Army surgeon, and pediatrician Dr. Richard Pan in California. In the GOP doctor's caucus, neurosurgeon Dr. John Cowan was elected in Georgia, but at least two incumbents lost their seats, with a few races still too close to call.

A big recruiting effort

Many of these new Democratic physician-lawmakers were recruited and backed by 314 Action, a name that refers to the mathematical constant pi. The organization supports progressive candidates with science backgrounds to run for office, and it invested more than $30 million in dozens of Democratic candidates competing in state and federal races, including 48 physicians.

The group's president, Shaughnessy Naughton, says that the organization does leadership development and recruits scientists to run across the country, then helps candidates in a variety of ways.

"We work to help them put together their campaign strategy, communication strategy, media training, we help to get them local and national media exposure, work with them on their fundraising, and fundraise for them," she explains.

Those candidates won big time on Tuesday. In addition to big national names like Senators-elect Andrews and El-Sayed, and Governor-elect Dr. Amy Acton of Ohio, many of the downballot candidates 314 Action supported won as well. Among them are several incoming state legislators who will be the only elected physicians in their chambers: Dr. Nikhil Wagle in Iowa, Dr. Amelia Gallitano-Mendel in Arizona, and Dr. Jarod Fox in Florida.

Naughton attributes that success to health care and affordability being front of mind. Also, polls show the public trusts doctors, and the candidates effectively countered messaging from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist who has downplayed ongoing measles outbreaks.

"People were sick of it," Naughton says. "We should not have American children dying — or anyone dying — of measles in 2026. And yet, not only did we have that happening, we had a health secretary that only made the situation worse."

A key vote, a damaging investigation

Outgoing chair of the powerful Health, Education, Labor and Pensions committee, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R.-La., spoke often from the dais about how his experience as a physician shaped his perspective as a lawmaker and committee chair.

During Kennedy's confirmation hearing in Jan. 2025, Cassidy memorably spoke about the root of his passion for vaccination. "In the early 2000's, I was loading a patient onto an air ambulance, an 18-year-old young woman, to go to get a liver transplant from acute liver failure due to hepatitis B," he said, noting the expensive surgery and ongoing hospital bills she would face, if she lived. "It was the worst day of my medical career, because I thought: $50 of vaccines could have prevented this all."

Still, Cassidy ultimately cast a key vote to confirm Kennedy into the job, despite Kennedy's long history of anti-vaccine activism. Kennedy flaunted vaccine-related promises Cassidy said he made to earn that vote, and even supported the Republican primary challenger who managed to unseat Cassidy earlier this year.

In a surprise Tuesday night, Dr. Roger Marshall, R.-Kan., also lost his reelection bid — another senior member of the HELP committee. Marshall is an OBGYN and staunch supporter of Kennedy. In September, the New York Times reported that Marshall had sued more than 700 patients for unpaid medical bills. One of the patients filed a class action lawsuit against him last week. Marshall described his actions as a way to "keep the lights on" in a last-minute social media video. He lost to challenger Adam Hamilton, a Methodist minister, by four points.

All the way back to 1776

Dr. Chadd Kraus has studied physicians in Congress. Kraus is now an emergency room doctor and the vice chair for research for the Department of Emergency and Hospital Medicine at Jefferson Health Lehigh Valley in Pennsylvania. Two decades ago, after studying political science as an undergrad and pursuing a masters in public health, he worked on an analysis of the physicians in Congress.

"In 1776, 10.7% of the signers of the Declaration of Independence were physicians," the paper notes. Kraus explains that was an era where practicing medicine involved leeches; germs hadn't been discovered and antibiotics hadn't been invented. Kraus suggests those physicians happened to be "part of a class that owned land that was educated."

In the next two hundred years, medicine transformed, and for a time, very few physicians served as federal lawmakers. "In the period of time that we studied [from 1960-2004], there were 25 physicians total who had served in the U.S. Congress, whether the House or the Senate," he explains. "In the current Congress, there are as many physicians — nearly — as there were in that whole period of time that we studied, which was several decades."

The new count

To be specific, there are 20 physicians in the current Congress, and Republicans outnumber Democrats two to one. There are six Democrats and 10 Republicans who serve in the House. All four doctors in the Senate are Republicans.

In the new Congress, there will be at least 18 physicians in Congress, 10 of them Democrats. Depending on the outcome of several House races, Democratic physician-lawmakers may outnumber Republican physician-lawmakers. Another notable win was in Ohio, where oncology nurse practitioner Kristina Knickerbocker flipped a Republican House seat. Nurse Lauren Underwood, a Democrat, held onto her House seat in Illinois.

In addition to Republicans Cassidy and Marshall losing their Senate seats, in the house, Rep. Neal Dunn of Florida, a urologist, retired, and Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, an ophthalmologist in Iowa, and Jen Kiggans, a nurse in Virginia lost their seats.

Kraus says, when it comes to making laws, "physicians have a valuable perspective, not a monopoly on good policy," he says. "And the need for physician voices in government has grown, I think, over the course of time, as healthcare has become more complex and politically consequential."

He says the emergency department, especially, is a place where you can see the effect of health policy in real time. He recalls at the beginning of the opioid crisis, how emergency physicians were among the first to sound the alarm to policymakers. When the uninsured rates increase, they see patients coming in sicker than they would otherwise be, he says. "We see the challenges of health policy and the consequences of it," he says

A health policy shake up?

Many of the new members of Congress campaigned on health policy issues, like the cost of health insurance and prescription drugs. There's widespread dissatisfaction with the cost of health care across the political spectrum. Democratic leaders have said that reversing Republican cuts to premium subsidies for health insurance and work requirements for Medicaid will be at the top of their agenda.

Beyond those immediate issues, more than 15 years after the passage of the Affordable Care Act, there may be political appetite and public demand for major new health legislation in the coming years. Some candidates ran on Medicare-for-all, a national health insurance plan, which has become increasingly popular in public opinion surveys.

"I think we all certainly agree, no matter one's political views or perspective, that there is the potential for a better system," Kraus says. "I do think that having physicians and other health care professionals meaningfully incorporated into the policymaking process is really critical to finding what those innovations might be."

Naughton of 314 Action says the health-professional candidates her group supported care about and have ideas about how to change the health care system, but that hasn't been their only pitch to voters.

"I do think that they really lead with what they essentially are, which is problem solvers," she says. "We can fix this problem — we can make health care accessible and affordable — and not make it a choice between life or debt."

Lexie Schapitl contributed reporting to this story.

entries.title: Navajo voters hop tractors, make extraordinary efforts to vote after widespread flooding
entries.summary: Four weeks of flooding washed out roads and sent thousands fleeing their homes on the Navajo Reservation. But many worked hard to get to polling places and voting day became part of the recovery process.
entries.content:
Navajo voters hop tractors, make extraordinary efforts to vote after widespread flooding

People on the Navajo Reservation had to make extra effort to vote this year.

It's a region of the southwest that's been hit this fall by repeated flooding. Roads washed out, driving thousands of people from their homes.

But voters turned out, in the parts of Arizona, Utah and New Mexico that the reservation stretches across. Yesterday at the Dennehotso Chapterhouse, voters rolled up in trucks with mud-caked tires.

The town is framed by the picturesque sandstone cursive of Comb Ridge, the stone spires of Monument Valley peeking over the ridgeline.

In the parking lot, people gathered to eat fry bread and mutton stew, something common at Navajo polling sites.

"I love to see our people come out and talk amongst each other," said 27-year-old Urbina Yazzie, adding that this year's election is unusual.

"People are having to drive on tractors to get from one road to another, just to come and vote," she said.

Dennehotso has been knocked around by floods this fall, three in the last month. But the big one that residents will talk about for decades to come, started on October 22.

Local contractor Kev Woolboy was helping coordinate response efforts, checking watersheds along the highway, as floodwaters from as far as 60 miles away raced toward town.

"We have some man-made earth dams that were supposed to slow (the water) down," Woolboy said. "But there was so much rain, those earth dams didn't stand a chance."

The floodwaters ravaged homes and newly-built roads, knocking out power and water, and leaving part of the town covered in thick, goopy mud.

"We thought we were safe," said 74-year-old Phyllis Yazzie.

Yazzie was at home with her son that day, having a late breakfast, when her niece called.

"And she says, 'Auntie! You better get out of there!'" Yazzie recalled. "I said, 'Why?' And she says, 'the flood's heading that way.' And so I went outside, I started looking towards the wash, and I saw the water rising.'"

They tried to drive out their dirt road, but were forced back to the highest point on their land, while a torrent of water carved ravines on both sides of their house.

"We parked the car and we spent the night in the vehicle," Yazzie said. "But they were trying to rescue us."

While Yazzie and her son huddled in their car, Kev Woolboy was working his way toward them, as the local guide for the Navajo Police Department, who had brought in an amphibious vehicle to rescue residents.

"I was jumping into the water and bringing the kids and some of the elders on board and helping them with their personal belongings," Woolboy said.

As it grew dark, and the flood waters rose, Woolboy says it became impossible to tell the difference between the ground and a swirling mix of rainfall and reddish brown silt.

They got close to Phyllis Yazzie's house, Woolboy asked the officers to stop the vehicle.

"I told the guys something doesn't look right," Woolboy recalled. "So they turned on their floodlights to where I could see. There was no road there. We had to turn around, we couldn't get Phyllis that night."

Two weeks later, residents were still digging out. On election day, a backhoe was building a a temporary road so that residents cut off from town could reach the polls at the Chapterhouse

Volunteer drivers, and Chapter employees were shuttling people there, too. Some people drove hours to get there.

Vera Begay was there, with her 92-year-old mother Lilien Begay, who lost her home and all of her identification documents.

"She's never missed her vote- all her life she's come here for voting," said Vera Begay.

The elder Begay, speaking in Navajo, said she is emotionally devastated.

This year in Dennehoto, and across the region, flooding has brought out the best in communities.

"It means a lot more to our people to come out and vote," said 27-year-old Urbina Yazzie. "Because this is a very very important time to do so, especially with the flood and all that's happening all over the Navajo Nation. It's tough out here."

But on election day, people who may disagree about politics were laughing and crying together, bringing their community back to life.

entries.title: Herbert Blomstedt, conductor of great orchestras for seven decades, dies at 99
entries.summary: Modest in his demeanor but remarkably enduring, the American-born, Swedish conductor continually fell in love with music, leading orchestras with no-nonsense insight and integrity well into his 90s.
entries.content:
Herbert Blomstedt, conductor of great orchestras for seven decades, dies at 99

Herbert Blomstedt, an American-born, Swedish conductor whose remarkably long career saw him leading many of the world's major orchestras, including the San Francisco Symphony for 10 years, died on Wednesday at his home in Gothenburg, Sweden. He was 99.

His death was announced in a statement released by his management company, KünstlerSekretariat am Gasteig.

In a profession routinely flush with elderly practitioners, Blomstedt, year after year, retained his title as the world's oldest active conductor. He worked into his late 90s, conducting concerts this year, at the age of 98, with the Detroit Symphony and the Gewandhaus Orchestra of Leipzig, Germany.

"Retirement is not a question of age," Blomstedt told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. "It should be flexible. I just love the music so much that I just can't give up." And he didn't.

Blomstedt suffered falls in 2022 and 2023, and an ear infection in 2025, forcing him to cancel performances in Europe and the U.S., but he was undaunted. He resumed adding dates to his schedule, leading the world's top orchestras. In recent years, he conducted while seated at a piano bench. He had plans to conduct a series of concerts with the San Francisco Symphony in May of this year and again in January 2027, both of which were canceled when health concerns got in the way.

"The music-making of elderly conductors can sometimes be either lofty or slow, sometimes both," Martin Kettle wrote in The Guardian in 2022. "Neither quality applies to Blomstedt … his conducting in old age radiates both flow and glow. Blomstedt does not force or underline the music, he releases it. But the attentiveness to pulse, phrasing and dynamics are unflagging."

Blomstedt brought clear-eyed structural integrity and a strict devotion to the composer's score to wide swaths of orchestral music — and eras — from J.S. Bach to Elliott Carter. But late in his career, he distilled his repertoire down to a few favorite Scandinavian composers and a handful of Germanic staples by Bruckner, Brahms, Schubert, Haydn, Mahler and his beloved Beethoven.

He recorded all nine Beethoven symphonies twice, once with the Staatskapelle Dresden, which he led from 1975 to 1985, and later with the Gewandhaus Orchestra of Leipzig, where he was chief conductor from 1998 to 2005.

"Both cycles remain beacons of good taste, with a distinctive spiritual power shining through," David Allen wrote in The New York Times in 2022. "That's particularly true of the Fifth [symphony], which may be less brutally violent than under other conductors but has a merciful empathy to its relative restraint." Asked by Allen why Beethoven remains such an obsession, Blomstedt pointed to the humanity in the composer's music.

"It can represent the suffering of everyone," Blomstedt answered. "Not only his, but mine. The suffering of today in Ukraine, for instance. That helps it outlive the personal situation of the composer, or the personal situation of the interpreter. It's something that we go through, as humans."

Herbert Thorson Blomstedt was born on July 11, 1927, in Springfield, Mass. to Swedish parents, both Seventh-day Adventist missionaries who returned home when Blomstedt was two, settling in Gothenburg.

In his youth, Blomstedt learned piano, violin and organ, then fell in love with symphonic music. He memorized the names of orchestra players and when the revered German conductor Wilhelm Furtwängler performed in Gothenburg, the shy young Blomstedt asked the maestro for an autograph.

In 1945, Blomstedt entered the Swedish Royal College of Music where he began to study conducting. His education continued with a broad range of influential figures, including stints with John Cage at Darmstadt, Igor Markevitch in Salzburg, Jean Morel at Juilliard and Leonard Bernstein at Tanglewood in 1953, the year in which Blomstedt won the Koussevitzky conducting prize. His formal conducting debut came in 1954 with the Stockholm Philharmonic, moving directly to his first professional post with the Swedish Norrköping Symphony Orchestra.

Blomstedt had close relationships with dozens of orchestras around the world, including the San Francisco Symphony, of which he was music director from 1985 to 1995.

"Blomstedt inherited an orchestra that was skilled and committed but lacking in discipline," says Joshua Kosman, former classical music critic for the San Francisco Chronicle. "Under his guidance, everything became sharper, cleaner, more crisply focused. It was also during his time as music director that the San Francisco Symphony began to tour internationally and record. These two developments were related. Blomstedt made the Symphony, as it were, ready for prime time."

In 2003, Blomstedt returned to lead the Symphony. Kosman said in a review at the time that it only took a few measures of music to realize how much the former music director was missed, especially in a performance of Schumann's Fourth Symphony.

"Looking spry and attentive, Blomstedt led a wonderfully vital performance," he wrote. "And the orchestra — clearly delighted to see its former music director — responded with some of its finest, most spirited playing."

While Blomstedt could elicit ecstatic performances from his orchestras, his own demeanor on the podium was calm and economical with no hint of spotlight-craving showmanship. At times, perhaps too much control led to the occasional indifferent performance. Another return visit to the Symphony in 2013 left Kosman cold. "The program began with the Prelude and "Liebestod" from Wagner's Tristan und Isolde, done with plenty of orchestral richness –- the strings sounded especially robust –- but not much fervor or freedom," he wrote. "Blomstedt is too rational and cautious an interpreter, I think, to make much of this music's luxuriant eroticism."

Blomstedt believed that music could be what he called "an enormous ethical force in society." Speaking with broadcaster Bruce Duffie in 1988, the conductor tried to explain its power. "I'm not so naïve that I think everybody who leaves the concert hall after a Bruckner symphony is saying, 'I won't do so many bad things tomorrow,' but something in that direction," he said. "To experience the order and beauty of great music brings the listener in contact with something greater than himself, something that is meant to be perfect and positive, and this is one of the greatest blessings of great music."

What Blomstedt sensed as something greater than himself was spiritual. A devout Seventh-day Adventist who eschewed alcohol, coffee, tobacco and meat, Blomstedt, early on, refused to rehearse on Saturdays, when he observed the sabbath. It cost him some jobs, he admitted. And yet he conducted concerts on those days, rationalizing that all the real work had been done in rehearsal and performing great music was a spiritual communication to the glory of God.

"I'm a seeker," Blomstedt told journalist Paul Bodine in 2004. "I find God in many places, in nature and scores, in people. I think the ultimate aim of every artist is not to project himself, but there is something in the music that he thinks is important, and when understood by listeners will bring them close to an answer to these eternal questions: Where we come from, why we are here, and where we are going?"

Blomstedt was married to Waltraud Blomstedt, also a Seventh-day Adventist, who held a degree in musicology. She died in 2003 at age 74 in Lucerne, Switzerland, where the couple had lived for years. Blomstedt moved back to Sweden, near Örebro, where three of his four daughters reside.

Earlier this year, the Danish Radio Symphony Orchestra announced plans for Blomstedt to conduct concerts during the three months leading up to his 100th birthday next July.

Always thinking about music and looking ahead, Blomstedt mused, in an interview with Die Welt in the fall of 2025, when he was 98, on what he might conduct for his centennial concerts. Mendelssohn, perhaps, he said. That same year, he told CBS News Sunday Morning, "Without work, I don't live. If I just twiddle my thumbs, that is not living." He said he wanted to be remembered as modest, but truthful and genuine.

"I'm not tired," he said firmly. "Because every time I stand in front of the orchestra, it's like a flame starts to sparkle again. The moment I hear the sound of the orchestra it transforms me."

entries.title: Chuck Schumer heralds Democrats' 'generational remake' of Senate
entries.summary: In remarks the day after his party flipped control of Congress, the Senate Minority Leader said voters had spoken clearly about their priorities, and said it's up to the Democratic party to deliver.
entries.content:
Chuck Schumer heralds Democrats' 'generational remake' of Senate

Midterms coverage: Live results | Takeaways | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told reporters Wednesday that the massive blue wave that brought Democrats control of the House and Senate signifies a "generational remake of the Senate map."

"These voters did not give us the majority so we can do whatever we want," the New York Democrat said outside the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee in Washington, D.C. "They entrusted us with the majority to do what they — the American people — want."

Democrats secured major gains in red states President Trump has previously carried, including Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. Their victories include a history-making win in Kansas, which hasn't sent a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years.

Schumer, who is poised to become Senate Majority leader in January, credited these wins to a crop of candidates who "knew how to tailor their message to the states."

Democrats now have a 54-seat majority, including the two independent senators who caucus with the party. Two races have still not been called: Alaska and Mississippi.

Schumer vowed that "relief is on the way" for voters, and acknowledged that some remain skeptical that Democrats will deliver. He said Democrats are intent on bringing down the cost of living, ending the Iran war, and undertaking investigations into the White House to address allegations of corruption.

"The days of Trump's supplicant Senate are over," Schumer declared.

President Trump hasn't shied away from saying he will use his veto pen on Democratic legislative priorities, but has also signaled some openness to cutting deals with the new Democratic-controlled Congress.

"We are going to work hard to drive costs down with the president or without him," Schumer said.

entries.title: Mike Johnson will step aside as top House Republican next Congress
entries.summary: After Tuesday's bruising defeat for Republicans, House Speaker Mike Johnson will not stay on as minority leader come January.
entries.content:
Mike Johnson will step aside as top House Republican next Congress

Midterms coverage: Live results | Takeaways | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

After a bruising defeat for Republicans, House Speaker Mike Johnson does not plan to stay on as Republican leader in the new Congress, according to a source familiar with his plans who was not authorized to discuss them publicly.

The Louisiana Republican served two terms as speaker, elected after his predecessor, California Rep. Kevin McCarthy, was ousted in 2023.

Johnson's decision will open a role for the top House leadership position in the minority. Republicans are scheduled to hold their leadership elections on Nov. 10.

Historically, the president's party loses seats in midterm elections. The blue wave soared past the expectations of many in Washington, flipping seats in traditionally red states that the president has won previously.

Johnson nodded to that history in remarks Tuesday night.

"From the first day of this election, we knew that to keep the House and sustain our majority, we would have to defy more than a century of midterm history. It's only happened twice in 90 years that a sitting president has picked up or held seats for his party in that first two-year cycle. There's a lot of reasons for it. It's very, very difficult to overcome, and it looks like history will be kept tonight," he said.

Johnson worked closely with the Trump administration throughout his tenure as speaker, and endured the balancing act of trying to keep his conference united with the narrowest of majorities. His razor thin majority meant even one Republican defection meant GOP priorities were at risk.

That dynamic will not be replicated for the presumptive next House Speaker, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York. While there are a handful of lawmakers elected with support of the Democratic Socialists of America, eager to push the party further to the left, the comfortable margin for Jeffries means he will likely be able to achieve his priorities, even with defections.

His speakership would be history making — he would be the first Black lawmaker elected to the position.

entries.title: Back in the majority, Democrats have plans for a long list of Trump investigations
entries.summary: Democrats will have the ability to subpoena records and compel individuals to testify. The Epstein files, Elon Musk, the Iran war and Trump's business interests may all come under the microscope.
entries.content:
Back in the majority, Democrats have plans for a long list of Trump investigations

Midterms coverage: Live results | Takeaways | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Democrats won big in the midterm elections, but with President Trump still in the White House, the next Congress is unlikely to see much major legislation signed into law.

Instead, expect to see a lot more oversight. With public corruption and failing leadership as two of the top issues concerning voters, congressional Democrats have an ambitious agenda of investigations planned for their return to power in the House and Senate.

Their new majorities mean that they will have at their disposal the full investigatory powers of the Congress, which include the ability to subpoena records for review and compel individuals to testify before lawmakers.

Rep. Robert Garcia, the California Democrat who is expected to become chair of the House Oversight committee, put it bluntly in a statement: "LAWYER UP."

The Democratic Party has a long list of investigative targets. According to conversations with Democratic House and Senate committee staffers, here are some areas the party is likely to prioritize in its oversight work.

Jeffrey Epstein

Among Democrats' primary targets: the administration's handling of — and connections to — the scandals of late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Bipartisan congressional action forced the Trump administration to release extensive documents tied to federal investigations of Epstein's crimes and other alleged offenses, though Democrats maintain that many of the records were improperly redacted or withheld from the public. They also say that the Justice Department has worked to shield Trump from damaging allegations — claims that the department's leadership has denied.

In the new Congress, lawmakers are expected to probe ties between Epstein and other powerful figures, including the president himself, which they say is part of an effort to secure accountability for victims of Epstein's crimes.

In connection with an October report, Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said, "Donald Trump says he knew Jeffrey Epstein 'just like everybody in Palm Beach knew him.' Not exactly."

"Evidence involving 11 women tells a completely different and far more damning story about their relationship and the abuse of young women and girls that took place in their network," Raskin said.

The president, for his part, has long denied any wrongdoing related to Epstein and has maintained that their relationship ended before the disgraced financier was indicted for soliciting prostitution in 2016.

Public corruption

Democrats also plan to continue their own investigations into what they describe as efforts by administration officials to advance the financial interests of the president, his family, themselves and close allies.

In particular, Democrats highlight the president's continued business interests, including Truth Social, a number of cryptocurrency projects and overseas projects involving his sons and powerful foreign investors.

Garcia on the House Oversight Committee, has gone further, linking the high cost of living to politicians on both sides of the aisle acting in their own self-interest rather than the interest of the American public.

"Millions of dollars in dark money are flowing throughout our political system. Some members of Congress may be trading stocks based on information the public doesn't have. The revolving door between the government and lobbying for large corporations keeps spinning," he wrote last month in an MS Now opinion piece. "Americans are dealing with a cost-of-living crisis, and these abuses of power are making it worse. All the while, the wealthiest people in our country are richer than ever."

Immigration

Trump returned to office promising a stricter approach to immigration in the United States. But public support for his deportation agenda has cratered in the wake of a number of high-profile incidents involving federal immigration enforcement personnel, including the killing of two U.S. citizens in Minnesota this year.

While in the minority, Democrats have publicly documented hundreds of incidents of alleged abuse and misconduct by immigration agents and will continue that work in the new term. They are expected to hold hearings on incidents of violence, which have largely gone without congressional oversight in the first two years of the president's second term.

Democrats held a field hearing in Austin, Texas, in October on shootings by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said following the hearing that "ICE is a lawless, rogue agency that is causing generational trauma in communities across the country. House Democrats today are doing the oversight work that Republicans refuse to do — and we will continue to do everything possible to protect our communities from Trump's mass deportation agenda."

Public health

In June, Democrats released a report documenting how they believe that the Trump administration has undermined public health infrastructure and U.S. scientific research into chronic and deadly diseases. That work will continue in the new year, with a particular focus on Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Executive power

Trump's muscular use of executive power has been unrestrained by the Republican congressional majority. That is expected to change.

Committee staffers indicate that the president's pet projects — remodeling the White House's East Wing, building a monumental arch, renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, shuttering the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, paving the White House's Rose Garden, among others — will face robust congressional oversight.

The projects are entwined in a larger constitutional fight over the appropriations process: Congress has the sole authority to decide how taxpayer dollars are spent, and the White House has repeatedly disregarded its declarations and rescinded billions of dollars in congressionally approved spending.

Iran war

Constitutional authorities delegated to Congress will also take center stage in Democrats' U.S.-Iran war oversight. The legislature has the sole authority to declare war, and presidents are required to seek authorization for the use of military force, something that has not happened for any of the Trump administration's military campaigns this term. Democrats also plan to press Pentagon officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, on the war's cost to the American public.

Even before the Democrats take control, a House impeachment vote on Hegseth could come during the lame-duck session.

More war powers votes — efforts to force the president to end the conflict, some of which have attracted limited bipartisan support — are also expected. While previous war powers votes have passed, the votes are largely symbolic and do not carry the weight of law.

Elon Musk

Technology titan Elon Musk has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican politics but has lately drawn the ire of Democrats after interruptions to his satellite internet service provider stymied Ukraine's military operations against Russia.

"We will ensure that the 120th Congress will closely scrutinize federal funding awarded to Mr. Musk's businesses, including whether these companies meet their contractual obligations, and whether adequate safeguards exist against political interference, arbitrary service restrictions, and misuse of federal resources," a group of Silicon Valley House Democrats wrote in a letter to the White House in October.

There could also be investigations into the Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency effort that decimated the government workforce in the first year of Trump's second term but failed to deliver on the promised trillion dollars in cost savings. It has remained a focus of House Oversight Committee Democrats during their time in the minority.

entries.title: Kansas just elected a Democrat. His message to Washington? Be decent
entries.summary: The Methodist pastor who flipped a Republican Senate seat says voters want more than political change. He tells NPR what he heard from Kansans about decency, faith and finding common ground.
entries.content:
Kansas just elected a Democrat. His message to Washington? Be decent

Adam Hamilton is the first Democrat since 1932 to win a U.S. Senate seat in Kansas

Adam Hamilton made history by becoming the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas since 1932. But the Methodist pastor says voters were looking for more than a change in party.

Speaking with NPR's Michel Martin on Morning Edition, Hamilton said rising costs, tariffs and the war in Iran helped drive his victory. He also heard something else: Americans are "sick and tired of the hyperpolarization in Washington."

Hamilton recalled meeting a Republican who said he had voted in 46 elections without ever supporting a Democrat — until Hamilton.

The voter told him Washington had become cruel and indecent.

In Greensburg, Kansas, a woman asked Hamilton to help Americans stop hating one another. She described family relationships fractured by politics.

"I really want you to help us remember that we're fellow human beings," Hamilton recalled her saying.

Hamilton, who was registered as a Republican until earlier this year, said Democrats should reach more religious voters and work across party lines.

He hopes to develop a close relationship with Kansas Republican Sen. Jerry Moran.

"I want to be his best friend in Washington," Hamilton said, describing his ambition to show that Republicans and Democrats can work together.

Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue button above.

The digital story was edited by Treye Green.
